subject: Follow-up: multiplexing window, ephemeral concurrency & quota proposal
messages:
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
To: Sana Patel <sana@finledger.com>
Cc: Jordan Blake <jordan@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 8 Jun 2026 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Follow-up: multiplexing window, ephemeral concurrency & quota proposal

Sana — great conversation earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our side. I want to make sure we document the performance profile you shared and surface the quota trade-offs we discussed.

Summary of FinLedger requirements (as we heard them)
- Active streaming sessions (websocket): ~480 concurrent active sessions during normal peak.
- Average sustained QPS to generation endpoints: ~120 req/s.
- Short burst behavior: peaks up to ~900 req/s for 20-60s during traffic surges (deploys & batch jobs).
- Latency targets: first-token p50 ~350ms, first-token p95 <= 850ms; streaming token p95 target <= 60ms. End-to-end completion p95 target ~800ms for short prompts.
- Typical request size: 32–128 tokens output, prompt sizes ~80–250 tokens.

Connection / concurrency model you prefer
- Lightweight multiplexing from frontend: pool persistent sockets at the edge and multiplex N sessions per connection (you mentioned ~4–8 multiplexed sessions per TCP/TLS socket).
- Idle session behavior: many sessions idle but must be able to ramp to active on user interaction within <200ms.

What Redwood needs to confirm / propose
- How many persistent connection slots to reserve (these are what we count against connection quota).
- Burst window sizing and throttling policy (per-account burst tokens).
- Whether idle-but-open websockets count toward the concurrency budget or we should count only active streams.

Initial ask from us
1) Please confirm whether the 480 concurrent sessions you shared are the expected peak for daily usage (if there are additional >2k one-off spikes during releases, flag them).
2) Share a 5–10 minute pcap/telemetry sample (or synthetic traffic profile) we can run through our latency simulator — anonymized is fine.
3) Would you prefer Redwood provide a pooled sockets quota (e.g., 150 sockets with 4 sessions each = ~600 logical sessions) or a straight session quota? We can model both.

Attached: redwood-connpool-proposal-v1.pdf (proposal sketch)

Proposed next steps
- We’ll run a quick simulator against your sample traffic and follow up with a recommended quota configuration and expected p95 latency under the proposed pooling scheme (deliverable within 48 hours once we have telemetry).
- If numbers look good, we can spin up a staged pilot (2-week) with reserved connection slots and a temporary burst increase.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
kimberly@redwood.com

From: Sana Patel <sana@finledger.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
Cc: ops@finledger.com
Date: Mon, 8 Jun 2026 18:03:00 -04:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: multiplexing window, ephemeral concurrency & quota proposal

Thanks Kim — helpful recap. A few clarifying questions before we send the telemetry: 

1) When Redwood says "connection slots", do you mean TCP/TLS sockets (we keep long-lived websockets from client to edge) or logical concurrent streams? We currently maintain ~1k open websocket connections across our fleet, but only ~400 are actively streaming at any moment.
2) Does Redwood charge against the quota for idle websockets (i.e., ones waiting for user interaction)? If so, can we distinguish idle vs active for billing and throttling?
3) For burst behaviour, we have a couple of predictable windows (deploy, marketing send) where 3–4x traffic for 45–90s is normal. Would Redwood be able to offer a short-term burst multiplier rather than permanently increasing our quota?
4) We use a multiplexing library that opens 1 connection per env host and multiplexes up to 6 logical sessions per connection. Is there an advantage to moving to fewer connections and higher multiplexing from Redwood’s perspective?

We can provide a 10-minute synthetic trace (anonymized) and a sample of average payload sizes. Planning to share that by EOD tomorrow.

— Sana
Sana Patel
Head of Integrations, FinLedger
Sana.Patel@finledger.com

From: Jordan Blake <jordan@redwood.com>
To: Sana Patel <sana@finledger.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 9 Jun 2026 09:10:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: multiplexing window, ephemeral concurrency & quota proposal

Sana — thanks for the quick questions. Answers inline and a concrete proposal below.

On Mon, Jun 8, 2026 at 6:03 PM Sana Patel <sana@finledger.com> wrote:
> 1) When Redwood says "connection slots", do you mean TCP/TLS sockets or logical concurrent streams?

We measure both but for quota purposes we can expose two surface areas: 
- Persistent connection slots (TCP/TLS / websocket sockets): straightforward to count.
- Active session concurrency (logical streaming sessions): counts live streams (where token emission is happening).

Practical recommendation: use persistent connection quota for headroom planning (idle sockets count against that quota). Then have a separate active session concurrency bucket for streaming throttles. That lets you keep many idle sockets without using up streaming concurrency.

> 2) Does Redwood charge against the quota for idle websockets?

We can treat idle sockets as part of the connection slot quota but not part of the active session quota. Billing/overage triggers are tied to active session concurrency and token units. If you prefer, we can tag idle connections and exclude them from short-lived burst enforcement for X minutes (configurable policy).

> 3) Burst windows: can we have a short-term burst multiplier?

Yes. We offer a burst token pool that can be sized to absorb 3x–5x historic peaks for configurable windows (30s–2min). Bursts consume the token pool first; once depleted the system falls back to throttles or queued requests depending on route policy.

> 4) Multiplexing strategy: fewer connections / higher multiplexing — pros/cons?

- Fewer sockets, higher multiplexing: fewer connection slots consumed, but risk of head-of-line blocking on the multiplexing layer during extreme bursts (depends on your library).
- More sockets, lower multiplexing: more predictable per-stream latency and isolation.

Concrete Redwood proposal (based on the profile you provided):
- Reserve connection slots: 150 persistent sockets (across your env host pool). Assuming your client multiplexes 4 sessions per socket, that maps to ~600 logical session headroom.
- Active session concurrency bucket: 600 active streaming sessions.
- Burst token pool: +700 transient session tokens (allows spikes up to ~1,300 active sessions for up to 90s).
- Sustained QPS guidance: we’ll provision for 200–300 sustained QPS for gen endpoints with token-based throttling on longer prompts.
- Latency expectations: with the above config and our optimized path we estimate first-token p95 <= 850ms and streaming-token p95 <= 60ms for the sample payloads you described (we’ll validate with your trace).

Attachments: connpool-simulated-latency.csv (simulation output) and redwood-connpool-proposal-v1.pdf (config summary).

Next steps:
- If you share the 10-minute synthetic trace, we’ll run it through the simulator and return a validated config + expected p95 numbers within 48 hours.
- Optionally: a 2-week staged pilot with those quotas provisioned (we provide a temporary burst multiplier and a short credit for testing).

If that sounds reasonable we’ll draft a short MOU for the pilot and schedule a technical deep dive with our infra team.

— Jordan
Jordan Blake
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Sana Patel <sana@finledger.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 10 Jun 2026 11:03:00 -04:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: multiplexing window, ephemeral concurrency & quota proposal

Thanks Jordan — that split between persistent sockets and active session buckets makes sense and aligns with our architecture. We will: 
- Share the 10-minute synthetic trace and average payload sample by EOD today.
- Prefer the 150-socket / 600 active session baseline with the +700 burst token pool for the pilot.
- We’d like to schedule the technical deep dive next Tue (16 Jun) at 09:00 PT if that works for your infra team.

I’m attaching our SOC2 answers document for your security/engineering review (finledger-soc2-answers.pdf). Please confirm the pilot MOU and any staging credentials you need.

Best,
Sana
